title: Synthetic Voting for the 2026 U.S. Senate Midterm Elections
section: The Democratic caucus is favoured to control the Senate, 52 seats to 48
text:
The Democratic caucus is favoured to control the Senate, 52 seats to 48
We combine synthetic responses from four language models with polling information to forecast the 35 Senate races in 2026. To estimate which party will control the Senate, we add the 35 race predictions to the 65 seats not up for election: 31 held by Republicans, 32 by Democrats, and two by independents, Bernie Sanders and Angus King, who caucus with Democrats.
The probability that the Democratic caucus reaches the 51-seat threshold for control, without support from newly elected independents, is 61 per cent; the probability that Republicans retain control is 37 per cent. Republicans need 50 seats because the Republican vice president can break a 50–50 tie. In 90 per cent of our simulations, Republicans win between 40 and 55 seats, showing the uncertainty around the forecast.



This summary shows all 100 Senate seats, with each model weighted equally. The Democratic caucus includes Sanders and King; any independent seats shown represent newly elected independents. Republican and newly elected independent seat counts are medians, with the remaining seats assigned to the Democratic caucus.



Democrats are favoured to gain North Carolina, Alaska and Ohio, now held by Republicans. Maine, Iowa and Texas are toss-ups, with each side given a winning probability of 45% to 55%.

title: Synthetic Voting for the 2026 U.S. Senate Midterm Elections
text:
How the forecast works
We forecast all 35 Senate races on 3 November 2026 by combining synthetic voter responses with polling information. We sample 100 personas per state from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Each persona receives nine news paragraphs, and four language models answer its voting question three times in their own words. We score these answers using Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR), then average the scores to estimate each state’s Republican share of the two-candidate vote.

On their own, the synthetic estimates lean about 5 to 9 points more Republican than the polls, partly because they reflect the personas’ 2024 votes rather than the shift since then. We therefore subtract each model’s average gap from the polls, then combine the corrected estimate with the state’s poll average. Where polls are unavailable, we use the weighted 2024 CES vote share plus the average shift observed in polled states. The noisier of the two estimates gets less weight. This adapts the inverse-variance weighting of Lock and Gelman (Lock and Gelman 2010), but our error estimates are approximate, and polls are not ground truth. We simulate 1,000 outcomes per model, allowing a shared national error to move states together, and give all four models equal weight. Adding the 65 seats not up for election produces a distribution over control of the 100-seat Senate. The Discussion compares this combined forecast with synthetic-only and no-LLM alternatives.

title: Synthetic Voting for the 2026 U.S. Senate Midterm Elections
text:
Methods
The voting responses are synthetic; we did not conduct a new survey. We used Python 3.12 (Python Software Foundation 2023) with pandas (McKinney 2010), NumPy (Harris et al. 2020), pyarrow (Apache Arrow Developers 2026), matplotlib (Hunter 2007), requests (Reitz 2026), lxml (Behnel et al. 2026) and tqdm (da Costa-Luis 2019), and sentence-transformers (Reimers and Gurevych 2019) for the pilot embeddings; tests use pytest (Krekel et al. 2004) and pandera (Bantilan 2020), and the website was built with Quarto (Allaire et al. 2026).

Data
Our personas come from the 2024 Cooperative Election Study (CES), a survey of 60,000 US adults (Schaffner et al. 2025; Ansolabehere et al. 2025). Of these respondents, 38,307 lived in the 35 states holding Senate elections in 2026. Among them, 23,025 had a post-election voter-file weight, and 21,211 were validated as having voted in 2024. We used the post-election weight because the persona characteristics draw on both survey waves. Having a voter-file weight does not itself establish that someone voted, so we applied the validated-voter restriction separately.
We obtained candidate lists from Wikipedia on 21 October (Wikipedia contributors 2026). Our two-candidate framework pairs the Republican with the leading Democratic or Independent opponent. Where several names were listed for a side, we used the candidate appearing most often in polls since 1 August. In Idaho, Nebraska and South Dakota, the opponent is Independent; in Montana, Independent Seth Bodnar polls ahead of Democrat Alani Bankhead. Additional candidates are acknowledged in the prompts but are not named individually.
We corrected Montana’s candidate pair before the 31 October run. The 27 and 29 October runs had paired Republican Kurt Alme with Bankhead rather than Bodnar, so their synthetic estimates and matched polls described a different contest. Those earlier Montana results are not directly comparable with the final run.
Polling data come from PollResults, which compiles Senate polls originally tracked by The New York Times (PollResults.org 2026). We use these data both in the combined forecast and as a benchmark for evaluating synthetic estimates. Polls are estimates of voter preferences, not election results; their role in setting the weights is discussed below.


Personas
Each persona describes a respondent’s age, education, race, gender, household income, ideology and party identification. Age is measured in 2024 and grouped as 18–29, 30–44, 45–64 or 65+. Education ranges from less than high school to a postgraduate degree. Race has five categories: White, Black, Hispanic, Asian and Other. Gender distinguishes men, women, non-binary respondents and other responses. Income retains the survey’s 16 brackets and its “Prefer not to say” option. Ideology ranges from very liberal to very conservative, while party identification distinguishes strong, weak and leaning partisans from Independents. Uncertain responses are retained as “Not sure.” The models do not see the respondent’s reported 2024 presidential vote, which we reserve for descriptive comparisons.


Weighted sampling
We draw 100 personas in each state, with replacement, giving respondents with larger survey weights a greater chance of selection. Using replacement in every state keeps the procedure consistent, including in Wyoming and Alaska, whose eligible pools contain only 52 and 76 respondents. Across the sample, 904 of the 3,500 personas repeat someone already selected in the same state. About two-thirds of the selections in Alaska and Wyoming are repeats, so 100 personas do not mean 100 distinct people.
The survey weights enter when personas are drawn rather than when their answers are aggregated. In contrast, Wang et al. (2015) adjusted an opt-in Xbox sample after collecting responses, using multilevel regression and post-stratification. Our weighted draw reproduces each state’s weighted CES composition in expectation, so each selected persona counts equally within its state. Applying the same survey weights again would double-weight the sample. This does not account for changes in the electorate between the 2024 presidential election and the 2026 midterms. Giving every state the same sample size supports separate race forecasts; pooled demographic comparisons require state-level weighting, as explained in Crosstabs.


News summaries
We collect news from publisher RSS feeds and use Google News site searches when needed. Each collection covers the preceding 48 hours, removes duplicates and keeps up to 60 items per outlet. The ten outlets are The New York Times, The Washington Post, The Wall Street Journal, USA Today, Fox News, New York Post, The Daily Wire, HuffPost, Mother Jones and Vox. Following Pew Research Center’s audience and political-leaning information (Shearer et al. 2025), we organise them into left-leaning outlets, newspapers and right-leaning outlets. “Newspapers” is a source group, not a claim of political neutrality.
GPT-4.1 Nano screens the titles and feed excerpts for US national significance and relevance to elections, policy, law or the economy, then writes a short paragraph for each retained item. The instructions exclude sports and other unrelated material and ask for a concrete development. Selected incorrect presidential and vice-presidential titles trigger a rewrite or exclusion. The resulting paragraphs are based on titles and excerpts rather than a full reading of each article; these checks do not independently verify the claims.
Each persona receives three randomly selected paragraphs from each source group, for nine in total. We join the existing paragraphs without asking a model to summarise them again. The same persona news block is used across models and repeat queries. A fixed random seed reproduces selections when the inputs are unchanged, and retries reuse the dated news selections. Example: the news block of one persona (Florida, 31 October)

Each of the 3,500 personas received nine paragraphs, three from each source group, drawn at random from that day’s kept articles (published 30 October 10:00 to 31 October 21:27 UTC). For illustration, we selected the archived block for persona FL_12, reproduced word for word. This example was not randomly selected and does not establish the quality of all news blocks.

Vox reports: Republicans are facing criticism for their vote to shrink Medicaid by roughly $1 trillion over the next decade, a move that is expected to leave more than 7 million Americans without healthcare coverage, impacting voter opinions in the 2026 midterm elections.
The New York Times reports: An article suggests that the upcoming election may bring significant political changes, regardless of the outcome of a Democratic sweep or not.
The Washington Post reports: A longtime Texas Republican reportedly split his ticket due to rising costs, reflecting economic concerns influencing voter and politician behavior.
The New York Times reports: Obamacare policies are experiencing steep premium increases for 2027, affecting nationwide healthcare affordability and policy discussions.
Fox News reports: A South Korean government-commissioned study suggests paper straws may pose health risks, scoring significantly higher than plastic on a cancer-related measure, raising questions about their environmental and health impacts.
Fox News reports: Mark Levin claims there was a conspiracy to steal the Senate, reflecting ongoing political debates and allegations concerning election integrity.
New York Post reports: The article discusses the possibility of military strikes against Iran by Israel, which could impact US foreign policy and security considerations.
Vox reports: A great deal is at stake in next week’s midterm elections. The partisan makeup of the new Congress will shape future spending bills, investigations, and judicial nominations, affecting US policy and governance.
HuffPost reports: JD Vance’s response to a young voter’s question about affordability has been criticized by experts, highlighting ongoing debates over economic policy.




Prompts and models
We ask each persona how it would vote in its state’s Senate race and randomise the order of the two candidates. We use models from four companies because their responses may differ systematically (Murray and Alexander 2026). We record the model identifier returned by the provider and the query time, since a model can change even when its advertised name stays the same (Bisbee et al. 2024).
We use Claude Haiku 5.5, GPT-6 Luna, DeepSeek V4.1 Flash and Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite through OpenRouter. Each model receives every persona’s prompt three times. We score the three responses separately and average their scores to reduce variation between individual answers. We ask for two or three sentences rather than percentages. We leave generation temperature at each provider’s default and cap output at 800 tokens. Reasoning is disabled except for Gemini, which requires it and uses minimal effort. Empty, refused and otherwise invalid responses are counted and excluded from scoring rather than treated as zero support. Four Claude Haiku calls returned no answer in the 31 October run; the cost table reports calls and answers by model.


Turning answers into voting probabilities

Why free-text answers?
LLM responses can concentrate too heavily on a small set of answers, a problem known as mode collapse. Heath and Alexander (2026) study whether free-text responses scored with Semantic Similarity Rating (SSR) better reproduce distributions in rating tasks. Maier et al. (2025) introduced SSR for purchase-intent ratings. We adopt the free-text approach for voting questions, while recognising that it does not by itself show that our responses avoid mode collapse.


Semantic Similarity Rating
Gemini Embedding 2 represents each answer and five candidate-specific statements as numerical vectors. The statements express definite support for the Democratic or Independent candidate, leaning toward that candidate, being undecided or choosing another option, leaning Republican, and definite Republican support. Cosine similarity compares the direction of the answer’s vector with each statement’s vector, producing five similarity scores per answer.
We rescale those five scores to the range zero to one and apply softmax with a temperature of 0.25. Adding the first two weights gives support for the Democratic or Independent candidate; adding the final two gives Republican support. The middle weight represents other choices, indecision or nonvoting. Answers and statements are embedded in the same way, without separate query and document settings.
These allocations are not calibrated probabilities of an individual’s actual vote. Vote choice is not an ordered rating scale, and the middle statement combines behaviours that may have different meanings. We do not apply a smoothing step or fit the temperature to voting outcomes, which we do not observe. This differs from the rating applications in Heath and Alexander (2026). Softmax can distribute weight to both sides even when an answer names one candidate clearly; that is a property of the scoring rule, not evidence of greater variation between personas.


Choosing the embedding model
On 26 October, we compared embedding models using 200 generated answers from Florida personas without news, 50 per voting model. Keyword rules identified 159 answers expressing a clear candidate choice. MiniLM placed 12 on the opposite side of the two-candidate scale; Gemini Embedding 2 misplaced one. The MiniLM errors were answers that supported Nixon but also mentioned Moody. Adding both names to each anchor made performance worse, so we retained single-candidate anchors and selected Gemini Embedding 2.
This was a limited diagnostic, not validation across all states. Neither setup captured indecision well: answers expressing it received an average weight of 0.14 on the middle category, while leaning and definite statements often received similar scores. These findings inform our choice of embedder but also show the limits of treating SSR weights as voting probabilities.



Combining synthetic votes with polls
We draw on Lock and Gelman’s (2010) inverse-variance approach to combining forecasts and polls. They estimate predictive uncertainty from past elections; we adapt the weighting idea to synthetic responses, using approximate error scales rather than reproducing their full Bayesian model.
We first average each persona’s scores over repeated answers. The state’s Republican two-candidate share is the mean Republican score divided by the sum of the mean scores for the two candidates. Resampling the personas 1,000 times gives a bootstrap measure of its variability. For the outside estimate, we use polls naming both selected candidates and ending within 45 days of the newest poll. We keep one question per poll, prefer likely-voter samples and average the two-candidate shares using sample-size weights. Where polls are unavailable, we use the weighted 2024 CES share plus the average shift in polled states, or “2024 plus swing.”

The combination has two steps. First, we remove each model’s bias, the mean difference between its synthetic share and the poll average across the polled states, giving the corrected share \(m^*\). Second, we average \(m^*\) and the outside estimate \(t\): the combined share is \(c=(1-w)m^*+wt\), with outside weight \(w=V_m/(V_m+V_t)\), so a larger synthetic variance gives the outside estimate more weight. The synthetic variance \(V_m\) is the bootstrap variance plus a structural variance, estimated from the polled states as the variance of \(m^*\) minus the poll average, after subtracting the average bootstrap and polling variances. We apply a floor of \(0.005^2\) to the structural variance so that it stays positive.
For polls, the error scale is sampling variance \(p(1-p)/n\) plus an assumed \(0.03^2\) for error beyond sampling (Shirani-Mehr et al. 2018). For states without polls, it comes from the errors around 2024 plus swing. Draws are normal around the combined share with variance \(1/(1/V_m+1/V_t)\), and a shared national error with standard deviation 0.03 is added. The weights assume that each model’s bias is the same in every state and that synthetic and polling errors are independent, so they are approximations. The Discussion compares the combination with synthetic-only and no-LLM forecasts, and with a version that keeps the bias and counts it as error instead.


Sources of uncertainty
The simulations reflect persona resampling, the structural synthetic error left after the bias correction, uncertainty in polls or the historical benchmark, and a national error that moves states together. Pooling the four models also retains their disagreements. However, the bias, the variances and the swing are estimated from the same polled states and treated as fixed, and we do not separately model regional errors or dependence between synthetic and polling errors. The sensitivity analysis shows how changing the assumed national and polling errors affects control of the Senate.


Tests
Before the full runs, we tested the workflow with five personas per state, free Laguna and Nemotron models, and a local MiniLM embedder. Separate test suites check the simulated data and the actual runs, using pytest and pandera. They check both individual tables and whether the sample, answers, scores and forecasts agree with one another.
We check that expected model–persona combinations and repeats are accounted for, failures are recorded, returned models match the requested provider, and token usage is available. Missing or refused answers must remain missing when scored. Valid scores must lie between zero and one and sum to one. Each forecast must assign valid vote shares and winners, fill all 100 Senate seats and keep the weighted estimate between its two inputs. A further check confirms that the combination uses the saved synthetic estimate and the recorded weights.
To check that the tests detect errors, we introduced missing probabilities, probabilities summing to 1.3, invalid vote-share totals and answers from another provider into a copy of the earlier data. Each was caught. Failed tests stop publication while preserving paid answers. These tests establish consistency of the calculations, not the accuracy of the election forecast.


Design
We used election coverage from CNN, Politico, NPR, CBC and Reuters as design references (CNN 2024; Politico 2024; NPR 2024; CBC News 2024; Reuters 2024). The website and figures share a colour palette, typography and table style so readers can compare results without relearning the presentation.

Evaluation
The forecast cannot be scored against the actual results until after the election on 3 November. Therefore, we compare it with a prediction market that forecasts the same races using a different method.

Against a prediction market
This comparison follows Wang et al. (2015), who forecast the 2012 presidential election using an opt-in poll of Xbox users. Before election results were available, they compared their state forecasts with prediction markets, which they described as among the most accurate sources of political forecasts. We use PredictIt (PredictIt 2026), which has a market for each of the 35 races and for control of the Senate. A contract pays one dollar if the predicted outcome occurs, so its price roughly reflects the market’s estimated probability. The two sides’ prices sum to slightly more than one, so we divide the Republican price by their sum, excluding third candidates as our forecast does. We use each market’s closing price on the date of each news run. Montana is excluded from the state comparisons on 27 and 29 October because our forecast used the Democrat Alani Bankhead instead of the independent Seth Bodnar (see Data); the Senate control comparison still uses the full forecast for each day. title: Synthetic Voting for the 2026 U.S. Senate Midterm Elections
text:
Discussion

Comparing synthetic-only, combined and no-LLM forecasts
The table compares four methods using the latest run’s saved inputs. Synthetic-only uses the original SSR shares without polling adjustment. The combined forecast—the headline result—removes each model’s average gap from the polls and averages the corrected shares with state polling averages where available. In states without usable polls, it instead combines them with the 2024 CES vote share shifted by the average change observed in polled states (“2024 plus uniform swing”). The third version skips the bias correction: it averages the raw synthetic shares and counts their gap from the polls as error, so the synthetic shares receive less weight but keep their lean. The no-LLM benchmark uses the same polling averages and 2024-plus-swing estimates, but excludes synthetic responses. This comparison shows how adding synthetic responses changes the forecast; it does not establish which method is more accurate before election results are available.

The synthetic methods pool four models with equal weight. Seat intervals contain the middle 90% of simulated outcomes.

For 31 October, adding polling and historical information lowers the Republican control probability from 90% in the synthetic-only forecast to 37%. The no-LLM benchmark gives 34%, so including synthetic responses moves the combined forecast toward greater Republican support. Synthetic estimates receive an average weight of 19% in polled states and 17% in unpolled states. The remaining weight goes to state polling averages or, where unavailable, the 2024 CES vote share plus uniform swing. The combined result is therefore driven mainly by these outside estimates. Without the bias correction, the synthetic shares receive less weight (an average of 11% in polled states) but keep their Republican lean, and the probability of Republican control is 42%: the choice between the two methods alone moves it by 5 points.



Do synthetic voters reproduce partisan voting patterns?
Argyle et al. (2023) describe algorithmic fidelity as a model’s ability to reproduce patterns of human responses across groups. We compare Republican support across demographic and party-identification groups: the synthetic responses for the 2026 Senate races alongside the same personas’ reported Republican vote in the 2024 presidential election. Their earlier vote was not included in the prompts. This asks whether the models reproduce earlier partisan patterns, rather than whether they correctly predict each person’s next vote. Some Senate opponents are Independents, so non-Republican support cannot always be labelled Democratic support.
Bisbee et al. (2024) caution that aggregate resemblance can coexist with overly uniform responses and distorted relationships between characteristics and opinions. Comparing party-identification groups helps show whether the models treat party as too decisive, while groups without a clear party preference provide a harder check. Close agreement with the 2024 column is not enough: turnout, candidates and voter preferences can change between elections. We therefore treat these tables as a description of the synthetic sample, not as evidence that its forecast is correct.


Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating
Our adaptation of SSR introduces measurement limitations separate from the variation in model answers (Heath and Alexander 2026; Maier et al. 2025). Softmax distributes weight across anchors even for an explicit candidate choice, so a group’s SSR share can be less one-sided than the share of its answers leaning toward that candidate. This within-answer allocation should not be interpreted as increased variation between personas or as evidence that mode collapse has been resolved. In the 26 October diagnostic check of 200 Florida answers, responses expressing indecision received an average p(other) of 0.14. That limited check suggests the combined undecided/other/nonvoting anchor may not capture indecision well; it does not establish scoring performance across all states. Both the anchors and the fixed temperature therefore remain sources of measurement uncertainty.



The news the personas read
Murray and Alexander (2026) find that party identification in a persona can limit the effect of news on its answers. Our news comparison shows relatively small changes in the average synthetic share across the recorded runs, although individual states move by different amounts. Every prompt states the persona’s party identification, which may help explain this stability. Because model answers also vary between runs, we cannot attribute the observed changes entirely to news exposure or conclude that news has no effect on real voters.



Uncertainty and the correlation between states
The sensitivity table shows that the probability of Senate control depends on the assumed size of shared national error, not just on the state point estimates. National shifts can move several close races together (Gelman et al. 2020). Regional patterns may matter too: an error concentrated in neighbouring states could produce outcomes that our single national component does not capture. The relatively small changes in the daily forecasts should therefore be read alongside their wide seat intervals, rather than as evidence of precision or accuracy.



What agreement with the market tells us
The market comparison shows close agreement across many states, but a high correlation can largely reflect agreement on safe seats. The differences in close races and in the probability of Senate control are more consequential. Neither approach is an independent test of polling information, since traders can read the same polls used in our combination. Thin trading and the treatment of long-shot outcomes can also affect prices (Rothschild 2009; Wang et al. 2015). Agreement is useful context, but election results are needed to assess accuracy.


Limitations
Unlike Lock and Gelman (2010), we do not have historical election errors for our synthetic forecasts from which to estimate their predictive uncertainty. Our error estimates are therefore an approximation developed for this project. We use polling data as a benchmark, but polls are not ground truth: sampling error, nonresponse, turnout assumptions and changes before Election Day can all affect them. Removing the average synthetic–poll gap treats the polls as correct on average: if the polls share an error, as they underestimated Republicans in 2016 and 2020, the correction carries that error into the forecast. Keeping the bias instead, as in the comparison version, hedges against this but leaves a known lean in the forecast; the choice alone moves the probability of Republican control by about 5 points (see Forecast by method). Polls inform the bias correction, the outside estimates and the combination weights. Agreement with polling benchmarks is not evidence of accuracy against election outcomes.

The fixed error estimates and omitted dependencies described in Sources of uncertainty may make the intervals too narrow. In the 10 unpolled states, the outside estimate assumes that every state moved the same distance from 2024, which ignores candidate effects, and the synthetic voters, whose weights are reported in the method comparison, bring their own state-specific errors. In Kentucky, where many personas identify as Democrats but describe themselves as conservative, synthetic estimates may differ systematically from the historical-vote benchmark. Such differences do not necessarily represent real candidate support. The 0.03 poll error beyond sampling is an assumption, so we also report results with 0.02 and 0.04. Relying on one aggregator (PollResults) does not remove errors shared across polls (Shirani-Mehr et al. 2018). The persona bootstrap also treats a respondent drawn twice as two different people, so in states with small pools, such as Alaska and Wyoming, it understates the uncertainty of the synthetic share.
In order to apply SSR, we had to flatten the candidate choices in each state to 2 sides to create a scale from Democrat to Republican, or from Independent to Republican, depending on which party the candidates belonged to. As a result, minor candidates and “don’t know” answers are not fully reflected in these results. Montana shows the cost most clearly: with the opposition split between an independent and a Democrat, a two-sided forecast leaves out about a sixth of the vote, and how Bankhead’s voters split between Bodnar and Alme, which may decide the race, cannot be modelled. The other limits of SSR are set out under Free text and Semantic Similarity Rating.
Provider defaults and model updates can limit reproducibility even with saved prompts. Due to cost, we collected news on only three days, which limits what we can infer about responses to changing events. Future work could vary the amount and mix of news while holding other inputs constant.

Historical election data from comparable synthetic forecasts would help test whether the estimated weights generalise beyond these runs.
Finally, the combination could be extended. The error scales could be allowed to differ by region or by how competitive a race is, the four models could be weighted against each other rather than reported separately, and the variances could be estimated jointly over the three news days rather than separately for each run.



Conclusion: what the synthetic voters add

Synthetic responses change the forecast relative to the no-LLM benchmark, but they receive a small share of the combined weight. This project therefore demonstrates a way to incorporate silicon sampling into an election forecast, rather than establishing that it improves on polling and historical information. The election results will provide a test of the recorded forecasts; broader evidence would require evaluation across more elections and settings.
